'''''Anju''''' ({{Korean/auto|hangul=안주|hanja=按酒|ko_ipa=an.dʑu}}) is a Korean term for food consumed with alcohol. It consists of a variety of foods, including both main dishes and [[banchan|side dishes]]. Consuming food with alcohol is a widespread practice in Korea, especially when the alcoholic beverage ''[[soju]]'' is involved.<ref name="Pettid">{{cite book|title=Korean cuisine: an illustrated history|year=2008|publisher=Reaktion Books Ltd|isbn=978-1-86189-348-2|pages=110–123|author=Pettid, Michael J.|location=China}}</ref><ref name="LAT">{{cite web|title=Food and drinks the Korean way|url=http://articles.latimes.com/2011/may/26/food/la-fo-anju-20110526|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110529094044/http://articles.latimes.com/2011/may/26/food/la-fo-anju-20110526|url-status=dead|archive-date=May 29, 2011|work=[[Los Angeles Times]]|access-date=30 April 2013|date=2011-05-26}}</ref>

Certain types of foods consumed primarily as ''anju'' include ''[[golbaengi muchim]]'', ''[[nogari]]'' with peanuts, and ''[[jokbal]]''.

==History==

Until the [[Joseon]] period, alcohol was mainly served in {{Transliteration|ko|[[jumak]]s}} (a type of inn or tavern), where soups with rice, along with traditional alcohol such as {{Transliteration|ko|[[makgeolli]]}}, were served to guests. Since the introduction of beer and Western foods into Korea, mainly from Japan in the nineteenth century, bars and pubs have enjoyed a newfound popularity, and many types of Western foods have been consumed as ''anju''.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://mnb.moneyweek.co.kr/mnbview.php?no=2015060317228021614|script-title=ko:왕맥의 안주 마케팅/'Wang-mec's anju marketing|last=Kang|first=Dong wan|date=2015-06-04}}</ref>

== By types of beverage ==
Some foods are considered to be best complemented by certain types of alcohol. For example, ''[[samgyeopsal]]'', grilled pork belly, is considered to go best with ''soju'', while fried chicken or Korean seasoned chicken goes well with beer. ''[[Pajeon]]'' and {{Transliteration|ko|makkeoli}} (or {{Transliteration|ko|dongdongju}}) is a popular combination for rainy days.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://m.insight.co.kr/newsRead.php?ArtNo=67691|script-title=ko:비 오는 날 '파전·막걸리'를 찾게 되는 진짜 이유|website=인사이트|date=18 May 2018 |language=ko|trans-title=Why we are looking for Pajeon in cloudy day|access-date=2019-05-31 |author1=서윤주 }}</ref>

==By the place where alcohol is served==
There are a number of different types of bar in South Korea, and each category sells different kinds of food and alcoholic beverage.

*{{Transliteration|ko|Jumak}}: this does not refer to the traditional Korean inns of the Chosun Dynasty mentioned above, but instead refers to a conceptual bar based on Korean culture. These bars are represented by traditional ''anju'' such as ''[[Pajeon|pa-jun]]'', ''[[dubu-kimchi]]'', or ''[[dotori-muk]]''.
*Hof house ({{IPA|ko|ho.pʰɯ ha.u.sɯ}}):<ref>{{Cite web|date=2014-06-04|title=Follies of Konglish|url=https://www.koreatimes.co.kr/www/opinion/2021/05/162_158502.html|access-date=2021-05-11|website=[[The Korea Times]]|language=en}}</ref> Hof houses (a German [[loan word]]) sell a number of relatively inexpensive alcoholic beverages. Various international dishes are served here as well.
*''[[Pojangmacha]]'': It is a place where tents are placed on the side of the road and snacks and alcohol are sold. Mainly simple side dishes are sold.
*[[Chimaek]]: Restaurants which serve fried chicken with beer.
